questions.question: A patient reports that right arm weakness and aphasia lasted 12 minutes this morning but are now completely resolved. What is the most appropriate FNP action?
choices: Schedule an outpatient MRI in several weeks
Treat as possible TIA or stroke and arrange urgent emergency evaluation
Reassure because symptoms resolved
Diagnose migraine without further assessment
questions.explanation: Transient focal deficits can represent TIA and carry early stroke risk. Resolution does not make the episode benign; emergency evaluation is required.

questions.question: What is the most important time to document when a patient may have acute stroke?
choices: The time the clinic opens
The last known well time
The time the patient completes the intake form
The time a family member becomes worried
questions.explanation: Last known well time helps emergency teams determine eligibility for time-sensitive evaluation and therapy. It is more useful than a vague estimate of when symptoms were noticed.

questions.question: Which presentation should raise concern for a posterior circulation stroke?
choices: Gradual knee pain after exercise
Sudden severe imbalance, diplopia, dysarthria, and vomiting
Chronic symmetric hand arthritis
Mild nasal congestion
questions.explanation: Posterior circulation events may present with sudden balance, eye movement, speech, coordination, or vomiting symptoms and require emergency assessment.

questions.question: Why should antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications not be treated as interchangeable after ischemic stroke?
choices: They have identical indications and risks
The appropriate strategy depends on stroke mechanism, bleeding risk, and specialist plan
Anticoagulants never prevent embolic stroke
Antiplatelets are used only for pain
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention is mechanism-specific. Antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and combination plans have different benefits and bleeding risks and should be verified from the discharge or specialty plan.

questions.question: A patient returns after stroke with aspirin, an anticoagulant, and two different statins listed in separate records. What is the best next step?
choices: Continue every listed drug indefinitely
Perform urgent medication reconciliation using discharge records and the responsible specialty plan
Stop all antithrombotics because of duplication risk
Ask the patient to decide which medication feels best
questions.explanation: Post-discharge lists are often incomplete or duplicated. Verify the event mechanism, intended drugs, duration, dosing, monitoring, and prescriber responsibility before making changes.

questions.question: Which statement about a normal single ECG after a cryptogenic stroke is most accurate?
choices: It excludes intermittent atrial fibrillation
It means anticoagulation is always indicated
It does not necessarily exclude intermittent atrial fibrillation, and rhythm evaluation may be extended
It proves carotid disease caused the stroke
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation may not appear on one ECG. The stroke team may pursue longer rhythm monitoring when no cause is identified.

questions.question: Which post-stroke assessment best identifies a hidden barrier to safe recovery?
choices: Ask only whether the patient can walk into clinic
Assess medications, cognition, swallowing, vision, mood, ADLs, caregiver strain, and driving or work needs
Repeat blood pressure only
Assume family presence means support needs are met
questions.explanation: Stroke recovery includes cognitive, communication, swallowing, visual, emotional, and social function. A patient can appear physically well but be unable to manage medications or remain safe at home.

questions.question: A patient on anticoagulation after cardioembolic stroke reports new severe headache and confusion. What is the appropriate disposition?
choices: Routine follow-up in 3 months
Emergency evaluation for possible intracranial bleeding or new neurologic event
Stop the medication without assessment and wait at home
Add an NSAID for headache
questions.explanation: New severe headache or neurologic symptoms in an anticoagulated patient can signal serious bleeding or recurrent stroke and warrants emergency assessment.

questions.question: Why is blood-pressure, lipid, diabetes, and tobacco management part of stroke care?
choices: These factors affect only the heart
They reduce recurrent vascular risk when integrated with mechanism-specific treatment
They can replace antithrombotic decisions
They are useful only before a first stroke
questions.explanation: Vascular risk-factor management is core secondary prevention. It complements, rather than replaces, mechanism-directed antithrombotic and procedural plans.

questions.question: What does closed-loop referral mean after a patient is discharged for stroke?
choices: A referral is placed without patient contact
The patient, records, clinical question, appointment, barriers, and follow-up responsibilities are confirmed
Primary care stops involvement after discharge
Rehabilitation is postponed until symptoms worsen
questions.explanation: Closed-loop care ensures referrals become completed care. Primary care coordinates records, medication safety, risk reduction, rehabilitation, and patient access.
